title: A Causal Framework for Estimating Heterogeneous Effects of On-Demand Tutoring
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of estimating causal effects for on-demand tutoring sessions embedded in adaptive learning systems. The authors argue that standard evaluations are confounded because students request help when they are already struggling, making naive comparisons between tutored and untutored attempts misleading. To solve this, they propose a causal inference framework that combines analytic sample construction, Deep Knowledge Tracing (DKT) to estimate latent student knowledge, and causal forests with doubly robust estimation to estimate both average and session-level heterogeneous tutoring effects.

The study is applied to more than 5,000 middle-school mathematics tutoring sessions from the Eedi adaptive learning platform. In Eedi, students worked on mathematics problems and could initiate brief synchronous text-chat sessions with human tutors. The sample came from a larger school-level randomized trial in which 12 schools and 2,585 students had access to the platform over two academic years, but the paper’s own analysis is observational at the tutoring-session level. Tutors were experienced teachers trained to support students through Socratic, problem-focused chat.

The authors find that requesting tutoring increases next-problem correctness by about 4 percentage points and improves accuracy on the next skill by about 3 percentage points. Effects vary substantially across sessions, ranging from strongly negative to strongly positive, and are larger for students with lower prior mastery, with slightly smaller effects for low-SES students. The paper concludes that DKT-informed causal forests can help estimate heterogeneous effects in embedded tutoring systems and could also support the evaluation and improvement of AI tutoring systems.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a strong observational causal-inference study with doubly robust estimation, causal forests, robustness checks, and placebo testing, but it is not a randomized evaluation of the tutoring interaction itself. The design credibly estimates heterogeneous session-level effects, yet residual confounding remains possible.
impact_tier_rationale: The estimated average effects are modest but meaningful for a priority population: +4.01 percentage points on immediate correctness and +2.73 percentage points on near transfer. The larger significance is methodological and operational, but the direct learning gains are in the modest-to-moderate range rather than large.

interventions.use_case: Causal evaluation framework for on-demand human tutoring embedded in an adaptive middle-school mathematics learning platform, using DKT and causal forests to estimate session-level effects and heterogeneity.
Eedi adaptive mathematics platform delivering diagnostic quizzes, hints, videos, and follow-up practice, within which on-demand tutoring was embedded.

finding.finding_summary: Across 2,585 middle-school students and 96,612 analytic problem attempts, on-demand tutoring increased immediate math correctness by 4.01 percentage points (ATE; 95% CI [2.51, 5.51]) and first-attempt accuracy on the next skill by 2.73 percentage points (95% CI [1.12, 4.35]). The paper also reports substantial session-level heterogeneity, with immediate-performance CATEs ranging from -20.25pp to +19.91pp and near-transfer CATEs ranging from -23.60pp to +47.70pp.
finding.measure: Next-problem correctness and first-attempt correctness on the subsequent skill (math problem accuracy)
finding.confidence_interval: [2.51, 5.51] for next-problem correctness; [1.12, 4.35] for near transfer
